title: The Boy Who Traded His Voice for Wings
summary: Finch hates his small, stammering voice, so he trades it to a sky-peddler for a pair of wings. Flying is everything he dreamed — until the night he sees the fire coming, and has no voice left to warn the people he loves.

chapters.title: The Voice He Hated
chapters.body:
Finch had a voice he could not stand.

It was small and it stammered. When he was nervous — and Finch was often nervous — the words caught in his throat like birds in a net, and came out broken, half-formed, in a whisper that made bigger children laugh. He'd learned to say as little as possible. He'd learned that a boy who doesn't speak can't be laughed at for how he speaks. And so Finch went quiet, and watched the sky instead, and wished more than anything that he could leave the ground and the laughter behind.

He lived in the hill-town of Kestrel, where the houses clung to a steep slope above a dry valley, and the wind came up strong from below. Finch would stand at the edge of the cliff after school and watch the hawks ride that wind, wheeling and soaring without a sound, and he would think: they don't need voices. They have wings. And no one laughs at a thing that can fly.

It was on one of those evenings, at the cliff's edge, that the sky-peddler came.

He came down out of the low clouds on a contraption of dark silk and bone, a thin man with a coat that rippled like feathers and eyes the pale grey of a winter sky. He landed light as a leaf beside Finch, and smiled, and his smile had too many teeth in it.

"A boy who watches the sky," the peddler said. "I know that look. You don't want to be down here. You want to be up there." He gestured at the wheeling hawks. "I can do that. I deal in flight. A pair of wings — real ones, your own — to carry you anywhere the wind goes."

Finch's heart leapt, and then he remembered to be careful, because even a quiet boy knows that things offered on cliff-edges by strangers have a price. "Wh-what would it c-cost?" he asked, and hated the stammer even as it happened, hated that the peddler had heard it.

The peddler's grey eyes glittered. "Ah," he said softly. "That. Your voice. That poor, small, stammering thing you hate so much." He leaned closer. "Why would you want to keep it? It brings you nothing but shame. It catches and breaks and makes them laugh. You barely use it as it is. Give it to me — the voice you already wish you didn't have — and I'll give you the sky. It's the best trade I offer. You lose only a thing you hate, and gain the one thing you dream of."

And Finch, who had spent his whole short life wishing his voice away, thought it was the easiest bargain in the world. What was a voice worth, if it only ever hurt him? What good had it ever done? He nodded — he couldn't even bring himself to say yes aloud, which felt like proof enough that the voice was worthless.

"Say goodbye to it, then," the peddler murmured. "One last word. Make it count."

Finch thought for a moment, and then whispered the only word that felt true: "Fly."

And the word left his throat and did not come back.

chapters.title: The Sky and the Silence
chapters.body:
The wings came in the night, and they were everything Finch had dreamed.

He woke to a strange new weight between his shoulders, and reached back, and felt feathers — his own, growing from his own back, brick-red at the tips and dark as ink at the roots. By dawn they were full-grown, and Finch climbed to the cliff's edge on trembling legs, and spread them, and stepped off into the wind.

And he flew.

It was better than watching. It was better than anything. The wind took him up and up, and the hill-town shrank below, and Finch wheeled and dove and soared with the hawks, silent as they were, free as they were. For days he did almost nothing else. He flew at dawn and at dusk and in the bright noon, and the ground and its laughter fell away beneath him, and he thought he had made the finest trade any boy had ever made.

But a silence, like all easy things, was easy to want at first and harder to live with.

The first time Finch noticed the cost was small. He landed one evening near two children he knew, meaning to greet them, to be — for once — the marvelous flying boy instead of the boy who couldn't speak. He opened his mouth. And nothing came. Not even the stammer. Just air. The children looked at him, waiting, and then shrugged and turned away, and Finch stood there with wings on his back and no way to say I'm here.

It happened again, and again. He could not call to his friends across the square. He could not answer when his grandmother asked how his day had been — he could only nod, or shake his head, and watch a small worry grow in her eyes that he had no words to soothe. He could not laugh out loud, could not sing, could not say thank you or I'm sorry or good morning. The wings carried him anywhere the wind went, exactly as promised. But a boy who can go anywhere and say nothing is still, in a way, more alone than a boy stuck on the ground who can at least call out to another person.

Finch began to understand what the peddler had known and not said. His voice had not been worthless. It had been small, and it had stammered, and it had brought him shame — but it had also been the one thread that tied him to everyone he loved. It was how his grandmother knew he was near. It was how he could reach another person across a distance. A voice, he understood too late, is not for sounding good. It is for reaching out. And he had traded his away for a pair of wings that could only ever carry him further from everyone.

He still flew. But now, at the top of his soaring, in the silent wind, he found himself looking down at the small warm lights of the hill-town, at the tiny figure of his grandmother in the doorway shading her eyes to watch for him, and he ached — with wings on his back and no way to call down that he was there, that he was safe, that he was coming home.

chapters.title: The Warning
chapters.body:
It was a dry-summer night when Finch, wheeling high above the sleeping hill-town, saw the fire.

It had started far down in the dead-dry valley — a spark, a lick of flame in the brush — and the strong wind that Finch loved so much was driving it up the slope, fast, toward the town where everyone he knew lay sleeping. From the ground, no one could see it yet; it was hidden behind the shoulder of the hill. But from the sky, Finch saw it plainly: a line of red creeping upward in the dark, and beyond it, unknowing, the houses of Kestrel with their shutters closed and their lamps out.

He had to warn them. And he opened his mouth to shout — the oldest instinct there is, to cry out danger — and nothing came. Just air. Just the silence he had traded for.

Finch dove for the town in a panic. He could fly; he could not call. He landed in the square and ran to the nearest door and pounded on it, but the family inside slept on, and when the father finally opened it, bleary and cross, Finch could only point, wild-eyed, at the hill — and the man saw nothing there, and could not understand the frantic silent boy, and shut the door. Finch pounded on another, and another, losing precious minutes at each, because a boy who cannot speak cannot say fire, cannot say run, cannot make a sleeping town understand in the seconds that matter.

And Finch understood, with a horror colder than the coming fire was hot, the true price of his trade. It had never been just about his own loneliness. A voice is how you warn the people you love. It is how you say danger, how you say help, how you reach across the dark to save someone. He had thrown that away because it embarrassed him — and now the people he loved might burn for it, because the flying boy could see the fire and could not shout.

But Finch was not going to let that be the end. If he could not use his voice, he would use the one thing he had traded it for.

He threw himself back into the sky, into the hot rising wind, and he flew — not away, for once, but straight at the danger. He flew to the great iron bell in the tower at the town's center, the alarm bell that hung silent because no one had ever needed it in Finch's lifetime, its rope long rotted away. There was no rope to ring it. So Finch did the only thing he could: he flew at the bell itself, and struck it with his whole body, wings and all, hurling himself against the cold iron again and again.

The bell rang.

Not a clean ring — a battered, desperate clanging, the sound of a boy throwing himself against iron over and over, bruised and gasping, his beautiful wings bent and torn with each blow. But it rang, and rang, and rang, loud enough to carry down every street of Kestrel. And the town woke. Shutters flew open. Lamps flared. And then they saw it — the red line climbing the hill — and the square filled with people, and the cry went up at last, from a hundred throats that still had voices: Fire! Fire! Wake up! Run!

The town emptied down the far slope in time. Every soul got out. The fire took some houses, and spared others, and by dawn the wind died and the rain came and it was over — and not one person of Kestrel was lost, because the bell had rung in the night.

Finch lay in the square as the sun came up, his wings broken and ruined from beating against the iron, and his grandmother found him there and held him, weeping, understanding without words — as she always had — what he had done.

The wings never healed right. In a few weeks they withered and fell away, feather by feather, and Finch was a boy on the ground again, earthbound, ordinary. He thought he would grieve them. And a little, he did.

But on the morning the last feather fell, something else came back. He was sitting with his grandmother, and she asked him — gently, the way she always had — how he was feeling. And Finch opened his mouth to nod, as he'd learned to do. And instead, small and cracked and stammering, a whisper climbed up out of his throat, rusty from disuse: "I'm… I'm h-here, Gran. I'm okay."

His voice had come back. Whatever the peddler had taken, the ringing of the bell — or the breaking of the wings, or simply the choosing of others over himself — had bought it back. And it was still small. It still stammered. It still caught in his throat when he was nervous.

But Finch never hated it again. Because he knew now what it was for. Not for sounding grand, not for escaping laughter — but for saying I'm here, and I love you, and, when it matters most, run. And there is no pair of wings in all the sky worth more than that.
